- Meteorological Overview: 

The next incoming trough coming down from Canada will bring an 
increase in winds aloft today. These stronger winds aloft will 
mix down to the surface from day time vertical mixing. The 
combination of the warm, breezy, and dry conditons will bring 
elevated to critical fire weather conditions to the region. 
Temperatures are also expected to peak today, with numerous lower 
elevation locations reaching into the 80s. 

Saturday, an elongated trough coming in from Canada will bring a 
multi-day weather system through Montana. A cold front passing 
from north to south Saturday morning bring the first rush of 
cooler air to the region along with mountain snow and lower 
elevation rain/snow. Lee troughing with northerly cold air 
advection continues behind the front, and transitions rain to snow
at lower elevations by Saturday evening. Meanwhile the front 
progression slows down heading into Southwest MT, which delays the
switch over the snow later than North-Central MT. Strong 
convergence and frontogenesis also occurs along this front as it
head into North-Central/Central MT, which can develop moderate to
heavy snow banding. Northerly flow in North-Central MT will allow
for enhanced snowfall for northerly upslope areas of the Little 
Belts/Central Continental Divide. Temperatures don't look to warm
up much heading into Sunday. Increasing moisture from the 
remnant southwest tropical storm system will continue to feed 
moisture into this storm system Sunday into Monday before exiting 
later in the day Monday.

Behind this system, another quick moving trough looks to swing 
through Wednesday into Thursday, which will keep the cooler 
temperatures and chances of precipitation. However, details with 
this will be heavily dependent on what happens this 
weekend/Monday. 

- Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

Cold Front and Temperatures Saturday and Sunday...

A strong cold front will move south from Alberta tonight and through 
the day on Saturday, with high confidence that the aforementioned 
front will bring a sharp drop in temperatures along with gusty north 
winds of between 35 to 45 mph to all locations upon its passage. At 
this time the following locations can expect the cold front to pass 
through between midnight and 3AM (Cut Bank), 3AM and 6AM (Great 
Falls), 6AM and 9AM (Havre), 9AM and noon (Lewistown, Helena, and 
White Sulphur Springs), noon and 3PM (Bozeman), and 3PM and 6PM 
(Dillon and Ennis). Should the cold front arrive sooner than 
expected at any given location then high temperatures for the day on 
Saturday will be much lower than currently forecasted, with a later 
arrival of the front having having the opposite effect on high 
temperatures (i.e. warmer than currently forecasted). The arrival 
time of the front will also be crucial in how quickly ground 
temperatures cool to support snowfall accumulations later on during 
the event, with an earlier arrival allowing for more time for the 
antecedent warm ground to cool. Be prepared for a significant change 
from the warm conditions as of late to more winter like temperatures 
this weekend


Snowfall Amounts from Saturday afternoon through Monday morning... 

Snowfall amounts over the past 12 hours continue to trend up over 
the plains of Central Montana along and south of the Montana Hwy 200 
corridor and north of the US Hwy 12 corridor, most notably in 
northerly upslope areas along and north of the Little Belt and Snowy 
Mountains where the flow is likely to become blocked leading to 
precipitation backing off of the adjacent terrain. While warm ground 
temperatures and the still "high" October sun angle will reduce 
snowfall accumulations on road surfaces and sidewalks, slippery and 
snow packed surfaces are still expected to develop due to the timing 
of the heaviest snow occurring from Saturday evening through Sunday 
morning. Additionally, periods of moderate to heavy snow, with 
snowfall rates of between 0.5" to 1" per hour, associated with an 
area of strong frontogenesis will help to offset the effects of the 
warm ground. In addition to the impacts to travel the wet and heavy 
nature of the snow could lead to tree damage, especially to those 
tress that still have foliage. Gusty north winds and the heavy, wet 
snow accumulating on power lines may also lead to isolated power 
outages; with the biggest concern for power outages occurring across 
the Southern Rocky Mountain Front and Montana Hwy 200 corridor.

Centennial Mountains, where the Winter Storm Watch was upgraded to a

Montana were upgraded to a Winter Storm Warning and extended through 
Monday morning. Additionally, the Snowy Mountains were also added to
